Hiroyuki Hirashita Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics, Academia Sinica, P.O. Box 23-141, Taipei 106, Taiwan hirashita@asiaa.sinica.edu.tw    Hidehiro Kaneda Institute of Space and Astronautical Science, Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, 3-1-1, Yoshinodai, Sagamihara, Kanagawa 229-8510    Takashi Onaka Department of Astronomy, Graduate School of Science, The University of Tokyo, 7-3-1 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo 113-0033    Toyoaki Suzuki Advanced Technology Center, National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, 2-21-1 Osawa, Mitaka, Tokyo 181-8588
Abstract

We report basic far-infrared (FIR) properties of eight blue compact dwarf galaxies (BCDs) observed by AKARI. We measure the fluxes at the four FIS bands (wavelengths of 65 μ𝜇\mum, 90 μ𝜇\mum, 140 μ𝜇\mum, and 160 μ𝜇\mum). Based on these fluxes, we estimate basic quantities about dust: dust temperature, dust mass, and total FIR luminosity. We find that the typical dust temperature of the BCD sample is systematically higher than that of normal spiral galaxies, although there is a large variety. The interstellar radiation field estimated from the dust temperature ranges up to 100 times of the Galactic value. This confirms the concentrated star-forming activity in BCDs. The star formation rate can be evaluated from the FIR luminosity as 0.01–0.5 M⊙subscript𝑀direct-productM_{\odot} yr-1. Combining this quantity with gas mass taken from the literature, we estimate the gas consumption timescales (gas mass divided by the star formation rate), which prove to span a wide range from 1 Gyr to 100 Gyr. A natural interpretation of this large variety can be provided by intermittent star formation activity. We finally show the relation between dust-to-gas ratio and metallicity (we utilize our estimate of dust mass, and take other necessary quantities from the literature). There is a positive correlation between dust-to-gas ratio and metallicity as expected from chemical evolution models.

1 Introduction

Dust grains absorb stellar ultraviolet (UV)–optical light and reprocess it into far-infrared (FIR), thereby affecting the energetics of interstellar medium. In particular, Hirashita & Ferrara (2002) show that the dust produced by supernovae efficiently absorbs UV heating photons and helps gas cooling and H2 production even in primeval galaxies (typical age is <108absentsuperscript108<10^{8} yr). Dust grains also affect the escape fraction of UV photons out of galaxies. Observationally, this means that there is always a correction factor for dust extinction when one estimates star formation rate (SFR) from UV luminosity (Buat & Xu, 1996). Indeed, a large correction factor for dust extinction is required for the cosmic star formation rate traced with UV (Steidel et al., 1999; Takeuchi, Buat, & Burgarella, 2005; Le Floc’h et al., 2005; Pérez-Gonzárez et al., 2005). Also theoretically, how dust accumulates in the history of the Universe is important in the context of the cosmic reionization, because dust absorption affects the escape fraction of ionizing photons (Ciardi, Bianchi, & Ferrara, 2002).

The origin of the cosmic dust is important in itself, and the formation and destruction of grains are tightly related to the star formation activity of galaxies. The condensation of heavy elements is an important process for the formation of grains. In particular, in young galaxies, dust is predominantly condensed in Type II supernovae (SNe II), whose progenitors have short lifetimes (Dwek & Scalo, 1980; Kozasa, Hasegawa, & Nomoto, 1989; Morgan & Edmunds, 2002; Nozawa et al., 2003). However, how much dust forms in a SN II is not known. There is a large difference among observationally derived dust mass (Moseley et al., 1989; Dunne et al., 2003; Hines et al., 2004; Sugerman et al., 2006; Meikle et al., 2007; Ercolano, Barlow, & Sugerman, 2007; Rho et al., 2008). Thus, it is important to constrain the dust mass formed in SNe II by quantifying dust mass in young galaxies.

A large amount of dust has been suggested to exist at high redshift (z𝑧z) (e.g., Bertoldi et al. (2003); Priddey et al. (2003)). The estimate of dust mass in high-z𝑧z galaxies indeed constrains how much dust forms in SNe II (Dwek, Galliano, & Jones, 2007). The rest-frame UV extinction curves also suggest that dust enrichment by SNe II is indeed occurring at high-z𝑧z (Maiolino et al., 2004; Bianchi & Schneider, 2007; Hirashita et al., 2008). However, it is not easy to explore the first dust enrichment in primeval galaxies at high z𝑧z (z​\gtsim​5𝑧\gtsim5z\gtsim 5) with present observational facilities. Therefore, nearby templates of primeval galaxies are useful to test galaxy formation scenarios. The best candidates for such a template are metal-poor (∼1/10similar-toabsent110\sim 1/10–1/3 solar) blue compact dwarf galaxies (BCDs), since they are at the early stage of chemical evolution and their typical stellar age is young (Sargent & Searle, 1970). Indeed BCDs harbor appreciable quantities of dust (Thuan, Sauvage, Madden, 1999; Plante & Sauvage, 2002; Hunt et al., 2006), and can be used to investigate the dust properties in chemically unevolved galaxies (Takeuchi et al., 2005).

The dust content in a galaxy is often estimated by measuring the dust emission in FIR. Because of the large all-sky sample, the Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS) 60 μ𝜇\mum and 100 μ𝜇\mum bands are most frequently used. However, Shibai, Okumura, & Onaka (1999), from the study of FIR spectral energy distribution (SED) of the Milky Way, show that the IRAS bands fail to detect a significant fraction of emission from large grains which contribute to wavelengths (λ𝜆\lambda) longer than 100 μ𝜇\mum (see also Okumura et al. (2002)). Moreover, with the size distribution derived for the Milky Way dust grains, the largest contribution to the dust content comes from large grains (a∼0.1​μsimilar-to𝑎0.1𝜇a\sim 0.1~{}\mum, where a𝑎a is the grain radius) (Mathis, Rumpl, & Nordsieck, 1977). Large grains also have an importance that their temperature reflects the stellar radiation field of interstellar medium through the equilibrium between the heating from stellar radiation and the radiative cooling in FIR (Draine & Anderson, 1985). In summary, FIR observation of emission from large grains at λ>100​μ𝜆100𝜇\lambda>100~{}\mum is important to quantify the dust content and the stellar radiation field.

Indeed, Galliano et al. (2005) show that some BCDs have a cold dust component contributing to λ>100​μ𝜆100𝜇\lambda>100~{}\mum. Popescu et al. (2002) also point out that BCDs tend to have the coldest dust temperature by using a Virgo cluster sample observed by the Infrared Space Observatory (ISO), although the sample size is small. This is unexpected from the warm IRAS 60 μ𝜇\mum/100 μ𝜇\mum colors of BCDs (Hoffman et al., 1989). Engelbracht et al. (2008), by using the 70 μ𝜇\mum and 160 μ𝜇\mum bands of Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS) on the Spitzer Space Telescope, show that the dust temperature tends to rise as the metallicity decreases from solar metallicity (Z⊙subscript𝑍direct-productZ_{\odot}) to ∼1/10​Z⊙similar-toabsent110subscript𝑍direct-product\sim 1/10~{}Z_{\odot}. However, there is a risk of contamination of stochastically heated dust in the 70 μ𝜇\mum band (Li & Draine, 2001), which leads to overestimation of the large-grain temperature. Thus, a statistical sample at λ>100​μ𝜆100𝜇\lambda>100~{}\mum is indeed required to avoid possible contamination from stochastically heated grains, and simultaneously to overcome the small number statistics of long-wavelength (λ>100​μ𝜆100𝜇\lambda>100~{}\mum) observations.

In this paper, we report observations of BCDs in FIR wavelengths including λ>100​μ𝜆100𝜇\lambda>100~{}\mum. The data are obtained by AKARI (Murakami et al., 2007) Far-Infrared Surveyor (FIS) (Kawada et al., 2007). The continuous wavelength coverage (λ∼50similar-to𝜆50\lambda\sim 50–180 μ𝜇\mum) and 4 bands in the FIR provided by FIS enable us not only to quantify the long-wavelength (λ>100​μ𝜆100𝜇\lambda>100~{}\mum) dust luminosity but also to separate the contribution from stochastically heated grains by using the short-wavelength (λ​\ltsim​70​μ𝜆\ltsim70𝜇\lambda\ltsim 70~{}\mum) band. We also demonstrate that this advantage of FIS indeed makes it possible to discuss some quantities related to dust properties and dust enrichment.

This paper is organized as follows. Observations and data reduction are described in section 2. Then, the basic data are shown in section 3, and some quantities derived from those data are presented in section 4. In section 5 we discuss the results, and finally in section 6 we summarize this paper.

2 Observations and Reduction

The observations of eight BCDs are carried out by FIS onboard AKARI as one of the open time observing programs (Proposal ID: BCDDE, PI: H. Hirashita) with four photometric bands of N60, WIDE-S, WIDE-L, and N160, whose central wavelengths are 65, 90, 140, and 160 μ𝜇\mum with effective band widths of Δ​λ=21.7Δ𝜆21.7\Delta\lambda=21.7, 37.9, 52.4, and 35.1 μ𝜇\mum, respectively (Kawada et al., 2007). The measured FWHMs of the point spread function (PSF) are 37±1′′plus-or-minus37superscript1′′37\pm 1^{\prime\prime}, 39±1′′plus-or-minus39superscript1′′39\pm 1^{\prime\prime}, 58±3′′plus-or-minus58superscript3′′58\pm 3^{\prime\prime}, and 61±4′′plus-or-minus61superscript4′′61\pm 4^{\prime\prime}, respectively, for the above four bands.

The sample BCDs are listed in Table 1. We primarily selected the sample with IRAS detections as listed in Hirashita, Tajiri, & Kamaya (2002) (originally compiled by Sage et al. (1992) and Lisenfeld & Ferrara (1998)). II Zw 40, Mrk 7, UM 439, UM 533, and II Zw 70 are finally observed. The limitation to the sample comes from the lifetime and visibility of the satellite. We also add Mrk 36 and Mrk 71 from Hopkins, Schulte-Ladbeck, & Drozdovsky (2002) since they matched the visibility requirement. Those galaxies are also detected by IRAS. II Zw 71 is also included in the sample, since it lies in the field of view of II Zw 70. This is the only galaxy which is not detected by IRAS. All the sample BCDs are observed with the FIS01 scan sequence (slow-scan observation for photometry), whose total area scanned in the four bands is 15′×12′superscript15′superscript12′15^{\prime}\times 12^{\prime}. Because of the faintness of the sample, we choose the slower scan speed (8 arcsec/sec) and the largest reset interval (2 sec). The observational parameters are also listed in Table 1.

The raw data were reduced by using the FIS Slow Scan Tool (version 20070914).111http://www.ir.isas.ac.jp/ASTRO-F/Observation/. The absolute calibration of the FIS slow-scan data is based on the COBE/DIRBE222http://cmbdata.gsfc.nasa.gov/product/cobe/. measurements of the diffuse sky emission from zodiacal light and interstellar cirrus averaged over areas of several slow-scan observations. Because the detector response is largely affected by a hit of high energy ionizing particle, we use the local flat; that is, we correct the detector sensitivities by assuming uniformity of the sky brightness (Verdugo, Yamamura, & Pearson, 2007).333We referred to AKARI FIS Data User Manual Version 2 available at http://www.ir.isas.ac.jp/ASTRO-F/Observation/. When we run the pipeline command ss_run_ss, we apply options /local,/smooth,width_filter=80: The flat field is built from the observed sky, and boxcar smoothing with a filter width of 80 s in the time series data is applied to remove remaining background offsets among the pixels. By using some relatively bright sources, we confirmed that the errors caused by the smoothing procedures are well within 10% for N60 (65​μ65𝜇65~{}\mum) and WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum) and 20% for WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum). These error levels are consistent to or somewhat larger than the background fluctuation mainly caused by a hit of high energy ionizing particle, which implies that the background fluctuation is a major component in the errors. The above values are adopted for the errors in Table 1 except for the following two cases: (i) For the N60 (65​μ65𝜇65~{}\mum) flux of Mrk 7, we adopt the root-mean-square (rms) of the background fluctuation. (ii) The uncertainty in the WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum) data of II Zw 70 is also large because of a bad pixel within the aperture radius (section 3.3). For N160 (160​μ160𝜇160~{}\mum), because of high fluctuation of the background, we adopt the 25% error after estimating the uncertainty in the background subtraction. When the flux is smaller than the rms of the background, we adopt 3 times the background uncertainty as an upper limit.

Our sample BCDs are compact enough to be treated as point sources with the resolution of FIS (but see section 3.3 for Mrk 71). We follow the aperture photometry described in Verdugo, Yamamura, & Pearson (2007). We adopt aperture radii of 0.625 arcmin for N60 (60​μ60𝜇60~{}\mum) and WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum) and of 0.750 arcmin for WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum) and N160 (160​μ160𝜇160~{}\mum), and sky regions between 2.25 and 3.25 arcmin for N60 (65​μ65𝜇65~{}\mum) and WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum) and between 3.0 and 4.0 arcmin for WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum) and N160 (160​μ160𝜇160~{}\mum). Then the aperture correction factors (1.58, 1.74, 1.71, and 2.03 for N60, WIDE-S, WIDE-L, and N160, respectively) are multiplied to obtain the total flux.444We also multiplied another factor called correction factor. It is an empirical factor to correct the discrepancy between the calibration of the diffuse emission (on which the present reduction is based) and that for point sources. This correction factor is empirically known to be constant. By using a different tool developed by T. Suzuki, who adopt point source calibrations by asteroids, we confirmed that the correction factors are reasonable within the errors put in this paper. See also Kawada et al. (2007) for the absolute calibration.

Finally, color corrections are applied for the WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum) fluxes: the color correction factor is assumed to be 0.93 (the flux is divided by this factors), which is valid for the temperature range derived by using 140 μ𝜇\mum and 90 μ𝜇\mum fluxes (22–53 K for β=1𝛽1\beta=1 and 19–36 K for β=2𝛽2\beta=2; see section 4.1) within 3%. For the WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum) band, color correction would be required. The correction factor is 0.94 at 35 K and 1.06 at 50 K for β=1𝛽1\beta=1, and 0.94 at 30 K and 1.06 at 40 K. These temperature ranges cover the average of 140 μ𝜇\mum–90 μ𝜇\mum temperature and 65 μ𝜇\mum–90 μ𝜇\mum temperature (section 4.1). For II Zw 71, whose temperature is significantly lower than the above ranges, upward ∼10%similar-toabsentpercent10\sim 10\% correction would be required. However, we do not apply color correction to the WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum) flux, because the emission in this band may not be described with a single-temperature emission and because the correction factor is not uniform within the sample (i.e., an iteration between the derived dust temperature and color correction is required for each object). For N60 (65 μ𝜇\mum) and N160 (160 μ𝜇\mum), we do not apply color correction, since the color correction change the flux only <4absent4<4% for our sample within the range of dust temperature derived for our sample in section 4.1.

3 Results

3.1 Flux

In Table 2, we present the measured fluxes. All the BCDs are detected in N60 (65​μ65𝜇65~{}\mum), WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum), and WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum) bands except for Mrk 36 (section 3.3). For the N160 (160​μ160𝜇160~{}\mum) band, a half of the objects are detected and only upper limits are determined for the other half. For comparison, in Table 2 we also compile the IRAS 60 μ𝜇\mum and 100 μ𝜇\mum fluxes if available. We adopt those data from Moshir et al. (1990) except for II Zw 40, Mrk 71 and II Zw 71 (section 3.3). For II Zw 40, we also present the data taken by Spitzer MIPS at λ=70​μ𝜆70𝜇\lambda=70~{}\mum and 160 μ𝜇\mum (Engelbracht et al., 2008).

3.2 FIR Spectral Energy Distributions

The data in Table 2 are displayed in Figure 1. For almost all the sources with available IRAS data, the AKARI and IRAS fluxes are consistent but there is a significant discrepancy between the IRAS 100 μ𝜇\mum flux (1.24±0.12plus-or-minus1.240.121.24\pm 0.12 Jy) and the AKARI 90 μ𝜇\mum (0.80±0.24plus-or-minus0.800.240.80\pm 0.24 Jy) flux for II Zw 70. Note that the error bar for the 90 μ𝜇\mum flux is large because of the bad pixel (section 2). However, we should note that the discrepancy seems significant even after considering the uncertainty in the interpolation. Another possible reason is that the IRAS flux is sometimes overestimated (Jeong et al., 2007). Source confusion could explain the discrepancy, but there is no evidence for a large sky fluctuation around II Zw 70 in our image.

The N160 (160​μ160𝜇160~{}\mum) flux, when detected, is always near to the WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum). Thus, the 160 μ𝜇\mum flux does not provide strongly independent information of the 140 μ𝜇\mum flux. Because of this and of a large fraction of non-detection, we do not use 160 μ𝜇\mum data in the following discussions. Nevertheless, it is worth stressing that the consistency between the 140 μ𝜇\mum and 160 μ𝜇\mum fluxes confirms the reliability of the N160 band. The N160 flux of II Zw 40 is also consistent with the Spitzer 160 μ𝜇\mum flux, which also strengthen the reliability of the N160 fluxes.

3.3 Remarks on individual objects

II Zw 40 — The IRAS data are taken from Vader et al. (1993) (see also Beck et al. (2002)). The Spitzer MIPS data are also available in Engelbracht et al. (2008).

Galliano et al. (2005) investigate this galaxy by using detailed SED models. They suggest a very cold dust contributing to the emission at λ​\gtsim​300​μ𝜆\gtsim300𝜇\lambda\gtsim 300~{}\mum (see also sections 4.5 and 5.2). However, we cannot constrain the dust emission at such a long wavelength range. Hunt, Bianchi, & Maiolino (2005) also study the SED over a wide wavelength range including FIR, and state that the FIR SED has a peak at λ​\ltsim​60​μ𝜆\ltsim60𝜇\lambda\ltsim 60~{}\mum, which is consistent with our data. This galaxy has the strongest interstellar radiation field, which supports high density of star formation (Beck et al., 2002; Vanzi et al., 2008).

Mrk 71 — This is called “cometary” BCD (Noeske et al., 2000) and given an NGC number NGC 2366. This is the nearest BCD of our sample with distance of 3.4 Mpc (Tolstoy et al., 1995). Indeed, an extended structure in the north-east direction from the main H ii complex NGC 2363 is seen in optical images. Since this paper treats the main star-forming region of a BCD, we concentrate on the main complex, which can be treated as a point source with the resolution of FIS. The north-east extension is detected in the N60 (65​μ65𝜇65~{}\mum), WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum), and WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum) band images. This extended structure does not affect our analysis because of its low surface brightness within the aperture used for the photometry.

With IRAS data, Mazzarella, Bothun, & Boroson (1991) derived larger FIR fluxes (4.829 Jy at λ=60​μ𝜆60𝜇\lambda=60~{}\mum and 5.713 Jy at λ=100​μ𝜆100𝜇\lambda=100~{}\mum) than our estimate. In the north-west extension, there is a brightness peak at distance of ∼3′similar-toabsentsuperscript3′\sim 3^{\prime} from the main body. The flux around this peak is preliminarily estimated as 0.7 Jy at λ=90​μ𝜆90𝜇\lambda=90~{}\mum and 0.5 Jy at λ=65​μ𝜆65𝜇\lambda=65~{}\mum. This peak can be contaminated with the main body with the resolution of IRAS (∼2′similar-toabsentsuperscript2′\sim 2^{\prime}–5′) (Neugebauer et al., 1984). Thus, we do not compare AKARI and IRAS results for this galaxy (section 3.2). A quantitative and detailed analysis of the north-east extension will be reported in a separate paper.

II Zw 70 — There is a bad pixel within the photometric radius in WIDE-S. Although the brightness of the pixel is extrapolated by using the value of the surrounding pixels, the uncertainty caused by this extrapolation may be as large as 30%.555We derived this error by using another analysis tool developed by Suzuki et al. (2008). Thus, we put a 30% error bar to the WIDE-S (90 μ𝜇\mum) flux.

II Zw 71 — This galaxy is occasionally detected in the same field of II Zw 70. It is located at the edge of the field of view, but the aperture used to determine the flux is well within the field. Although the area for the background is smaller than the other sources, the number of background pixels is large enough to subtract the background within errors of 10% for N60 (65​μ65𝜇65~{}\mum) and WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum), 20% for WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum), and 25% for N160 (160​μ160𝜇160~{}\mum). This galaxy is not detected by IRAS.

Mrk 36 — This is the faintest object in WIDE-S. This galaxy is detected by IRAS at λ=60​μ𝜆60𝜇\lambda=60~{}\mum with a flux level of 0.022±0.05plus-or-minus0.0220.050.022\pm 0.05 Jy and is not detected at λ=100​μ𝜆100𝜇\lambda=100~{}\mum with an upper limit of 0.680.680.68 Jy (Moshir et al., 1990). In the WIDE-L image, it seems that relatively bright pixels are clustered in the expected position of Mrk 36. If we use those clustered bright pixels and subtract the background, the flux is 0.15 Jy. But since the uncertainty in the background is comparable to this value, it is safe to put an upper limit of 0.30 Jy.

4 Derived Quantities

4.1 Dust temperature

One of the most straightforward quantities derived by our observations is colors (i.e., flux ratios between two bands), which reflect dust temperatures. In Table 3, we show the colors. Since the WIDE-S (90 μ𝜇\mum) band is the most sensitive, we present the color relative to 90 μ𝜇\mum flux. We denote the flux ratio between wavelengths λ1subscript𝜆1\lambda_{1} [μ𝜇\mum] and λ2subscript𝜆2\lambda_{2} [μ𝜇\mum] as [λ1subscript𝜆1\lambda_{1}, λ2subscript𝜆2\lambda_{2}]. The error of a flux ratio f1/f2subscript𝑓1subscript𝑓2f_{1}/f_{2}, where we denote the errors of f1subscript𝑓1f_{1} and f2subscript𝑓2f_{2} as err(f1subscript𝑓1f_{1}) and err(f2subscript𝑓2f_{2}), respectively, is estimated by using a simple discussion of error propagation as

(1)

We compare the derived colors with other available samples of star-forming galaxies observed by AKARI FIS. To date, FIS observations of three spiral galaxies have been published to date (Kaneda et al., 2007; Suzuki et al., 2007) as shown in Table 3. We observe that the derived colors of the BCDs show higher temperatures (i.e., larger [65, 90] and smaller [140, 90]) than the spiral galaxies except for Mrk 7 and II Zw 71. This supports the idea that BCDs host intense star formation activities in concentrated regions.

We have selected the present sample primarily from the IRAS catalog. Since intense star formation tends to raise FIR luminosity, our sample may be biased to objects with intense star formation. Indeed, II Zw 71, which is not detected by IRAS, has the lowest dust temperature, and this fact implies a possibility that our selection by IRAS detection is biased to high dust temperature.

Note that A𝐴A can be eliminated if we take a flux ratio. If Td​([65/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]6590T_{\mathrm{d}}([65/90]) is equal to Td​([140/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]14090T_{\mathrm{d}}([140/90]),666When the parameter β𝛽\beta is omitted, the statement is true for any β𝛽\beta. the fluxes in the three bands can be fitted with a single dust temperature. The difference between Td​([65/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]6590T_{\mathrm{d}}([65/90]) and Td​([140/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]14090T_{\mathrm{d}}([140/90]) is significant for Mrk 7 and II Zw 71 if β=1𝛽1\beta=1, and for Mrk 7, Mrk 71, UM 439, UM 533, and II Zw 71 if β=2𝛽2\beta=2. In those BCDs, Td​([65/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]6590T_{\mathrm{d}}([65/90]) is higher than Td​([140/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]14090T_{\mathrm{d}}([140/90]), which possibly indicates that the contribution from stochastically heated grains to the 65 μ𝜇\mum flux is prominent compared with the short-wavelength tail of the emission at λ>90​μ𝜆90𝜇\lambda>90~{}\mum (Draine & Li, 2001). Since the emission at λ>90​μ𝜆90𝜇\lambda>90~{}\mum comes from dust grains in temperature equilibrium between the heating from stellar radiation field (called interstellar radiation field) and the cooling by FIR reemission, observations by the WIDE-S and WIDE-L bands are essential to estimate the equilibrium grain temperature. In such a case, the dust temperature derived from the IRAS 60 μ𝜇\mum and 100 μ𝜇\mum bands is overestimate for the equilibrium grain temperature. For BCDs in which Td​([65/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]6590T_{\mathrm{d}}([65/90]) is consistent with Td​([140/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]14090T_{\mathrm{d}}([140/90]), on the contrary, the IRAS 60 μ𝜇\mum and 100 μ𝜇\mum bands have given reasonable estimate for the equilibrium dust temperature. In this case, the Spitzer 70 μ𝜇\mum and 160 μ𝜇\mum bands also provide the equilibrium grain temperature.

It is worth noting that as demonstrated above the AKARI FIS bands have the following two advantages: One is that two bands, WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum) and WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum), are available to estimate the equilibrium grain temperature, while the Spitzer 70​μ70𝜇70~{}\mum and 160 μ𝜇\mum bands have risk of overestimating the equilibrium grain temperature because of the contribution from stochastically heated grains to λ=70​μ𝜆70𝜇\lambda=70~{}\mum. (But a wide band has a disadvantage in determining the flux density. In fact the color correction factor is relatively large for WIDE-S (90 μ𝜇\mum) and WIDE-L (140 μ𝜇\mum) as stated in section 2.) The other is that the N60 band (65​μ65𝜇65~{}\mum) is also crucial to estimate the contribution from stochastically heated grains. Thus, the three bands of FIS adopted in this paper provide a unique opportunity to investigate both equilibrium-temperature dust and stochastically heated dust.

4.2 Interstellar radiation field

Since the dust temperature is determined by the equilibrium between the heating from interstellar radiation field and the cooling by FIR reemission, it is possible to estimate the interstellar radiation field from the equilibrium dust temperature. We adopt Td​([140/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]14090T_{\mathrm{d}}([140/90]) as the equilibrium grain temperature. The 140 μ𝜇\mum–100 μ𝜇\mum color of the Galactic disk is concentrated around 2.0 (Hibi et al., 2006; Hirashita, Hibi, & Shibai, 2007), which corresponds to the dust temperature of 20.2 K for β=1𝛽1\beta=1 and 17.3 K for β=2𝛽2\beta=2. Assuming that the dust heating is dominated by UV radiation (Buat & Xu, 1996), we estimate the UV radiation field from the dust temperature. The UV radiation field normalized to the Galactic value is denoted as GUVsubscript𝐺UVG_{\mathrm{UV}}. Using the scaling relation of GUV∝Td4+βproportional-tosubscript𝐺UVsuperscriptsubscript𝑇d4𝛽G_{\mathrm{UV}}\propto T_{\mathrm{d}}^{4+\beta} (Evans, 1995), we obtain

GUV​(β)={(Td20.2​K)5if β=1, (Td17.3​K)6if β=2.subscript𝐺UV𝛽casessuperscriptsubscript𝑇d20.2K5if β=1, superscriptsubscript𝑇d17.3K6if β=2.\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{UV}}(\beta)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\left({\displaystyle\frac{T_{\mathrm{d}}}{20.2~{}\mathrm{K}}}\right)^{5}&\mbox{if $\beta=1$, }\\ \left({\displaystyle\frac{T_{\mathrm{d}}}{17.3~{}\mathrm{K}}}\right)^{6}&\mbox{if $\beta=2$.}\\ \end{array}\right. (4)

In Table 4, we present GUV​(β)subscript𝐺UV𝛽G_{\mathrm{UV}}(\beta) for β=1𝛽1\beta=1 and 2. Naturally we confirm the above conclusion that the UV interstellar radiation field in BCDs is systematically higher than that in spiral galaxies, although Mrk 7 and II Zw 71 are exceptions. Moreover, there is little difference in GUVsubscript𝐺UVG_{\mathrm{UV}} between β=1𝛽1\beta=1 and 2. Thus, it is more useful to adopt GUVsubscript𝐺UVG_{\mathrm{UV}} instead of Tdsubscript𝑇dT_{\mathrm{d}} to avoid the dependence on β𝛽\beta.

4.3 Total FIR luminosity

Total FIR luminosity reflects how much stellar light is absorbed and reemitted by dust grains. It is empirically known that FIR luminosity is a good indicator of SFR in galaxies (Kennicutt, 1998; Inoue, Hirashita, & Kamaya, 2000). Here we estimate the total FIR luminosity of each BCD. The FIS N60 (65​μ65𝜇65~{}\mum), WIDE-S (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum), and WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum) bands have the advantage of covering continuously the wavelength range from 50 μ𝜇\mum to 170 μ𝜇\mum (Kawada et al., 2007). Thus, by using those three bands, we define the AKARI FIR flux, fAKARIsubscript𝑓AKARIf_{\mathrm{AKARI}}, as an estimate of the flux in the above wavelength range:

fAKARIsubscript𝑓AKARI\displaystyle f_{\mathrm{AKARI}} ≡\displaystyle\equiv fν​(65​μ​m)​Δ​ν​(N60)subscript𝑓𝜈65𝜇mΔ𝜈N60\displaystyle f_{\nu}(65~{}\mu\mathrm{m})\Delta\nu(\mbox{{N60}}) (5)

+fν​(140​μ​m)​Δ​ν​(WIDE-L),subscript𝑓𝜈140𝜇mΔ𝜈WIDE-L\displaystyle+f_{\nu}(140~{}\mu\mathrm{m})\Delta\nu(\mbox{{WIDE-L}})\,,

According to Kawada et al. (2007), we adopt Δ​ν​(N60)=1.58Δ𝜈N601.58\Delta\nu(\mbox{{N60}})=1.58 THz, Δ​ν​(WIDE-S)=1.47Δ𝜈WIDE-S1.47\Delta\nu(\mbox{{WIDE-S}})=1.47 THz, and Δ​ν​(WIDE-L)=0.831Δ𝜈WIDE-L0.831\Delta\nu(\mbox{{WIDE-L}})=0.831 THz. With fAKARIsubscript𝑓AKARIf_{\mathrm{AKARI}}, we define the AKARI FIR luminosity, LAKARIsubscript𝐿AKARIL_{\mathrm{AKARI}}, as an estimate of the luminosity in λ=50𝜆50\lambda=50–170 μ𝜇\mum:

LAKARI≡4​π​D2​fAKARI,subscript𝐿AKARI4𝜋superscript𝐷2subscript𝑓AKARI\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{AKARI}}\equiv 4\pi D^{2}f_{\mathrm{AKARI}}\,, (6)

where D𝐷D is the distance to the object. In Table 4, we list the estimated AKARI FIR luminosities as well as the distances. The distances are taken from Tolstoy et al. (1995) for Mrk 71 (NGC 2366), Osman, Ella, & Issa (1982) for NGC 2841, Karachentsev et al. (2002) for NGC 2976, and Jurcevic & Butcher (2006) for M 101. For more distant galaxies, we estimate the distance from the Galactocentric velocity (taken from NED)777http://nedwww.ipac.caltech.edu/. by assuming a Hubble constant of 75 km s-1 Mpc-1.

It is convenient to obtain a conversion formula from the AKARI FIR luminosity to the total FIR luminosity. We define the “correction” factor, CAKARIsubscript𝐶AKARIC_{\mathrm{AKARI}}, which is to be multiplied to the AKARI FIR luminosity to obtain the total FIR luminosity as

LFIR​(β)=CAKARI​(β)​LAKARI,subscript𝐿FIR𝛽subscript𝐶AKARI𝛽subscript𝐿AKARI\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{FIR}}(\beta)=C_{\mathrm{AKARI}}(\beta)L_{\mathrm{AKARI}}\,, (10)

Because the sample size is small, we cannot investigate the possible dependence of CAKARIsubscript𝐶AKARIC_{\mathrm{AKARI}} on various physical parameters such as dust temperature. Thus, we only estimate the average of CAKARIsubscript𝐶AKARIC_{\mathrm{AKARI}} for the sample. The results are listed in Table 5, where the averages of CAKARIsubscript𝐶AKARIC_{\mathrm{AKARI}} with and without the spiral sample are shown. We see that there is no significant difference in CAKARIsubscript𝐶AKARIC_{\mathrm{AKARI}} between those two averages. On the other hand, there seems to be difference in CAKARIsubscript𝐶AKARIC_{\mathrm{AKARI}} between β=1𝛽1\beta=1 and 2, mainly because the extrapolation to long wavelengths (λ>170​μ𝜆170𝜇\lambda>170~{}\mum) in estimating the total FIR luminosity depends on β𝛽\beta. In summary, we can convert the AKARI FIR luminosity to the total FIR luminosity by multiplying 1.2–1.4. We note that a further 30–40% correction for the contribution from mid-infrared emission at λ<50​μ𝜆50𝜇\lambda<50~{}\mum will be necessary to estimate the total infrared luminosity of dust emission (Dale & Helou, 2002).

4.4 Star formation rate

It is empirically known that the FIR luminosity is a good indicator of the SFR. Hirashita, Buat, & Inoue (2003) provide a conversion formula from LFIRsubscript𝐿FIRL_{\mathrm{FIR}} to SFR (we assume that LIRsubscript𝐿IRL_{\mathrm{IR}} in Hirashita, Buat, & Inoue (2003) is approximated by LFIRsubscript𝐿FIRL_{\mathrm{FIR}}, but as mentioned in section 4.3, the upward 30–40% correction for λ<50​μ𝜆50𝜇\lambda<50~{}\mum may be required for LFIRsubscript𝐿FIRL_{\rm FIR}):

SFR=CIR​LFIR,SFRsubscript𝐶IRsubscript𝐿FIR\displaystyle\mathrm{SFR}=C_{\mathrm{IR}}L_{\mathrm{FIR}}\,, (11)

where we adopt the conversion coefficient CIR=2.0×10−10​M⊙​yr−1​L⊙−1subscript𝐶IR2.0superscript1010subscript𝑀direct-productsuperscriptyr1superscriptsubscript𝐿direct-product1C_{\mathrm{IR}}=2.0\times 10^{-10}~{}M_{\odot}~{}\mathrm{yr}^{-1}~{}L_{\odot}^{-1} as recommended by Hirashita, Buat, & Inoue (2003). The SFR estimated by using LFIR​(β=1)subscript𝐿FIR𝛽1L_{\mathrm{FIR}}(\beta=1) is listed in Table 6 for each galaxy. If we adopt LFIR​(β=2)subscript𝐿FIR𝛽2L_{\mathrm{FIR}}(\beta=2), we obtain smaller SFR by 4–26%. The range of the SFR is 0.01–0.4 M⊙subscript𝑀direct-productM_{\odot} yr-1 for the present BCD sample. This is within the range (a few times 10−3superscript10310^{-3} to several times 10 M⊙subscript𝑀direct-productM_{\odot} yr-1) given for a BCD sample by Hopkins, Schulte-Ladbeck, & Drozdovsky (2002).

There are two common BCDs between this paper and Hopkins, Schulte-Ladbeck, & Drozdovsky (2002): Mrk 71 and Mrk 36. For the latter galaxy, we do not obtain the SFR because it is not possible to determine LFIRsubscript𝐿FIRL_{\mathrm{FIR}} (section 4.3). For Mrk 71, our estimate is 2–3 times lower than their estimate (0.065 M⊙subscript𝑀direct-productM_{\odot} yr-1 from the IRAS 60 μ𝜇\mum luminosity and 0.041 M⊙subscript𝑀direct-productM_{\odot} yr-1 from the 1.4 GHz radio luminosity). This confirms the comment of Hirashita, Buat, & Inoue (2003) that there is a risk of underestimating the SFR for SFR​\ltsim​1​M⊙SFR\ltsim1subscript𝑀direct-product\mathrm{SFR}\ltsim 1~{}M_{\odot} yr-1 if we use equation (11). This may be because of smaller dust optical depth.

There are three overlapping BCDs between this paper and Sage et al. (1992): II Zw 40, UM 439, and UM 533. Their SFR derived from the FIR luminosity (0.46, 0.085, and 0.049 M⊙subscript𝑀direct-productM_{\odot} yr-1, respectively) is systematically higher, which is attributed to different CIRsubscript𝐶IRC_{\mathrm{IR}} (6.5×10−9​M⊙​yr−1​L⊙−16.5superscript109subscript𝑀direct-productsuperscriptyr1superscriptsubscript𝐿direct-product16.5\times 10^{-9}~{}M_{\odot}~{}\mathrm{yr}^{-1}~{}L_{\odot}^{-1}). This high CIRsubscript𝐶IRC_{\mathrm{IR}} is consistent with the SFR derived from Hα𝛼\alpha luminosity in dwarf galaxies (Thronson & Telesco, 1986), which again confirms the necessity of using higher CIRsubscript𝐶IRC_{\mathrm{IR}} than proposed by Hirashita, Buat, & Inoue (2003) for SFR​\ltsim​1​M⊙SFR\ltsim1subscript𝑀direct-product\mathrm{SFR}\ltsim 1~{}M_{\odot} yr-1 . Moreover, the SFR derived from Hα𝛼\alpha in Sage et al. (1992) (3.1, 0.20, and 0.19 M⊙subscript𝑀direct-productM_{\odot} yr-1, respectively) is much higher than SFR derived from the FIR luminosity, which is again explained by small dust optical depth as mentioned in the previous paragraph. However, the SFR derived from Hα𝛼\alpha luminosity in Sage et al. (1992) could be overestimated because they assume that 2/3 of the ionizing photons are absorbed by dust, which might be less in low-metallicity galaxies like BCDs.

4.5 Dust mass

As stated in section 1, the WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum) and WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum) bands are suitable to trace the total mass of large grains which have the dominant contribution to the total dust content. The total dust mass Mdsubscript𝑀dM_{\mathrm{d}} is related to the flux as (e.g., Hildebrand (1983))

Md=Fν​(λ)​D2κν​Bν​(Td),subscript𝑀dsubscript𝐹𝜈𝜆superscript𝐷2subscript𝜅𝜈subscript𝐵𝜈subscript𝑇d\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{F_{\nu}(\lambda)D^{2}}{\kappa_{\nu}B_{\nu}(T_{\mathrm{d}})}\,, (12)

where κνsubscript𝜅𝜈\kappa_{\nu} is the mass absorption coefficient of dust grains. For simplicity, we assume spherical grains with a single radius a𝑎a and with a uniform density s𝑠s. As shown later, the assumption on a𝑎a is not essential, since κνsubscript𝜅𝜈\kappa_{\nu} is insensitive to a𝑎a. The cross section of a grain is expressed as π​a2​Qν𝜋superscript𝑎2subscript𝑄𝜈\pi a^{2}Q_{\nu}, where Qνsubscript𝑄𝜈Q_{\nu} is a dimensionless quantity expressing the emission efficiency. Using Qνsubscript𝑄𝜈Q_{\nu}, the mass absorption coefficient is written as

κν=3​Qν4​a​s.subscript𝜅𝜈3subscript𝑄𝜈4𝑎𝑠\displaystyle\kappa_{\nu}=\frac{3Q_{\nu}}{4as}\,. (13)

Since there is a relation of Qν∝aproportional-tosubscript𝑄𝜈𝑎Q_{\nu}\propto a for a≪λmuch-less-than𝑎𝜆a\ll\lambda (Evans, 1995), the estimate of κνsubscript𝜅𝜈\kappa_{\nu} is insensitive to the assumed value of a𝑎a. Hildebrand (1983) estimates Qν/asubscript𝑄𝜈𝑎Q_{\nu}/a at λ=125​μ𝜆125𝜇\lambda=125~{}\mum to be 3/400 μ𝜇\mum-1. We note that the normalization of Qν/asubscript𝑄𝜈𝑎Q_{\nu}/a at λ=125​μ𝜆125𝜇\lambda=125~{}\mum is convenient since it is roughly the middle of the two wavelengths (λ=90​μ𝜆90𝜇\lambda=90~{}\mum and 140 μ𝜇\mum) used for the estimate of dust mass. If we adopt s=3𝑠3s=3 g cm-3, we obtain

κν=18.8​(λ125​μ​m)−β​cm2​g−1.subscript𝜅𝜈18.8superscript𝜆125𝜇m𝛽superscriptcm2superscriptg1\displaystyle\kappa_{\nu}=18.8\left(\frac{\lambda}{125~{}\mu\mathrm{m}}\right)^{-\beta}~{}\mathrm{cm}^{2}~{}\mathrm{g}^{-1}\,. (14)

In Table 4, we list the dust mass, where we adopt Td​([140/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]14090T_{\mathrm{d}}([140/90]) for the dust temperature. The dust mass estimated with β=1𝛽1\beta=1 and 2 are denoted as Md​(β=1)subscript𝑀d𝛽1M_{\mathrm{d}}(\beta=1) and Md​(β=2)subscript𝑀d𝛽2M_{\mathrm{d}}(\beta=2), respectively. The dust mass in Mrk 36 is given by using the Td​([65/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]6590T_{\mathrm{d}}([65/90]) instead of Td​([140/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]14090T_{\mathrm{d}}([140/90]), for which only a lower limit is given. Since Td​([65/90])subscript𝑇ddelimited-[]6590T_{\mathrm{d}}([65/90]) tends to overestimate the equilibrium grain temperature (section 4.1), we regard this dust mass to be a lower limit. From Table 4, we observe that Md​(β=1)subscript𝑀d𝛽1M_{\mathrm{d}}(\beta=1) is systematically lower than Md​(β=2)subscript𝑀d𝛽2M_{\mathrm{d}}(\beta=2) by a factor of 2.5. This is because higher dust temperature for β=1𝛽1\beta=1 leads to a lower dust mass with a fixed dust emissivity.

One of our BCDs, II Zw 40, overlaps with the sample in Galliano et al. (2005) (section 3.3), who model the dust SED. First of all, the mass of the big grain component, which is contributing to the FIR regime, is just the same as our estimate (1.1×105​M⊙1.1superscript105subscript𝑀direct-product1.1\times 10^{5}M_{\odot}) if we adopt β=2𝛽2\beta=2. This means that the AKARI WIDE-S (90​μ90𝜇90~{}\mum) and WIDE-L (140​μ140𝜇140~{}\mum) bands are indeed useful to trace the dust mass. However, they also show an additional very cold dust component contributing to the emission at submillimeter wavelengths, although the amount of this component is dependent on the FIR emissivity index β𝛽\beta. This very cold component cannot be investigated by AKARI, and we concentrate on the dust component contributing to the FIR emission in this paper.

5 Discussion

5.1 Star formation properties

In section 4.2, we have shown that the BCD sample tends to show higher UV radiation fields than spiral galaxies. This is consistent with a picture that intense star formation is occurring in a concentrated region in BCDs. In order to examine the properties of such an intense star formation activity (e.g., a burst or a continuous mode of star formation) it is useful to estimate the gas consumption timescale (τSFsubscript𝜏SF\tau_{\mathrm{SF}}) as follows.

Here, we adopt the SFR estimated in section 4.4 by adopting LFIR​(β=1)subscript𝐿FIR𝛽1L_{\mathrm{FIR}}(\beta=1). (If we adopt LFIR​(β=2)subscript𝐿FIR𝛽2L_{\mathrm{FIR}}(\beta=2), the gas consumption timescale becomes 4–26% shorter.) Then the gas consumption timescale is defined as the gas mass divided by the SFR. For the gas mass, we adopt the mass of H\emissiontypeI gas (MH​\emissiontype​Isubscript𝑀H\emissiontype𝐼M_{\mathrm{H}\emissiontype{I}}) in the same way as in Hirashita, Tajiri, & Kamaya (2002) and Hopkins, Schulte-Ladbeck, & Drozdovsky (2002), since molecular gas is rarely detected for BCDs (Barone et al., 2000). We estimate MH​\emissiontype​Isubscript𝑀H\emissiontype𝐼M_{\mathrm{H}\emissiontype{I}} of II Zw 71 by using the H\emissiontypeI flux measured by Huchtmeier & Richter (1989) and by using equation (1) in Lisenfeld & Ferrara (1998). The estimated gas consumption time τSFsubscript𝜏SF\tau_{\mathrm{SF}} is listed in Table 6. We observe that τSFsubscript𝜏SF\tau_{\mathrm{SF}} is distributed with a range of two orders of magnitude, which is consistent with Hopkins, Schulte-Ladbeck, & Drozdovsky (2002). Moreover, the gas consumption time does not correlate with GUVsubscript𝐺UVG_{\mathrm{UV}}. For example, Mrk 71 has large GUVsubscript𝐺UVG_{\mathrm{UV}}, which indicates a concentrated intense star formation, but has large τSFsubscript𝜏SF\tau_{\mathrm{SF}} exceeding the cosmic timescale. Such galaxies with long τSFsubscript𝜏SF\tau_{\mathrm{SF}} but high GUVsubscript𝐺UVG_{\mathrm{UV}} give us a picture that the star formation is strongly activated only in a limited region. On the contrary, II Zw 40 has large GUVsubscript𝐺UVG_{\mathrm{UV}} and small τSFsubscript𝜏SF\tau_{\mathrm{SF}}, indicating the whole galaxy may be in an active phase of star formation.

It is possible that the star formation in BCDs is intermittent. In this case, the diversity in τSFsubscript𝜏SF\tau_{\mathrm{SF}} is naturally explained: if a BCD is in activated/inactivated phase of star formation, τSFsubscript𝜏SF\tau_{\mathrm{SF}} becomes small/large. Indeed, the effect of feedback is considered to be enhanced in small systems such as BCDs, leading to an intermittent nature of star formation (Saitō, Kamaya, & Tomita, 2000; Carraro et al., 2001; Kobayashi & Kamaya, 2004; Kamaya, 2005). It is also observationally suggested that the star formation in dwarf galaxies may be episodic (Fanelli, O’Connell, & Thuan, 1988; Greggio et al., 1998; Grossi et al., 2007).

5.2 Dust-to-gas ratio and chemical enrichment

The dust production is strongly related to the metal production. Indeed, the relation between dust abundance (usually dust-to-gas ratio is adopted) and metal abundance (metallicity) can be investigated by using chemical evolution models (Dwek, 1998; Hirashita, Tajiri, & Kamaya, 2002). Here we consider whether dust-to-gas ratio and metallicity are related or not.

As the metal abundance, we adopt oxygen abundance, which is the most easily observed. The oxygen abundance of each sample BCD is compiled in Hirashita, Tajiri, & Kamaya (2002) and Hopkins, Schulte-Ladbeck, & Drozdovsky (2002), but for II Zw 71 we take the oxygen abundance from Kewley, Jansen, & Geller (2005). The dust-to-gas ratio 𝒟𝒟{\cal D} is estimated by Md​(β=1)subscript𝑀d𝛽1M_{\mathrm{d}}(\beta=1) divided by MH​\emissiontype​Isubscript𝑀H\emissiontype𝐼M_{\mathrm{H}\emissiontype{I}}. If we use Md​(β=2)subscript𝑀d𝛽2M_{\mathrm{d}}(\beta=2) instead, we obtain about 2.5 times higher dust-to-gas ratio. Note that the dust-to-gas ratio would shift further upward if there is really a very cold dust component contributing to longer wavelengths than those traced by AKARI (Galliano et al. (2005); section 4.5). In Table 6, we list the metallicity (oxygen abundance: 12+log⁡(O/H)12OH12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})) and the dust-to-gas ratio 𝒟𝒟{\cal D}. Note that the solar abundance is 12+log⁡(O/H)=8.9312OH8.9312+\log(\mathrm{O/H})=8.93 (Anders & Grevesse, 1989).

In Figure 2, we show the relation between those two quantities. We observe that there is a positive correlation between dust-to-gas ratio and metallicity. This correlation is also shown by Engelbracht et al. (2008) with a larger metallicity range. The correlation is consistent with the picture that dust enrichment proceeds as the system is enriched by metals.

It is also interesting to compare the results with theoretical model predictions. Here we adopt a model by Hirashita, Tajiri, & Kamaya (2002) (originally developed by Lisenfeld & Ferrara (1998)), who consider a one-zone chemical evolution model with the instantaneous recycling approximation (Tinsley, 1980). The model equations consist of the evolutions of gas mass, metal mass, and dust mass. By treating these equations, the relation between dust-to-gas ratio and metallicity is obtained. In particular, there are two important parameters in the model: (i) the fraction of metals condensed into dust grains, finsubscript𝑓inf_{\mathrm{in}}, and (ii) the “dust destruction efficiency”, βSNsubscript𝛽SN\beta_{\mathrm{SN}}. The former parameter is fixed to 0.1, and does not contribute to the scatter of the dust-to-gas ratio if the condensation efficiency in the stellar mass loss is independent of age. The “dust destruction efficiency” βSNsubscript𝛽SN\beta_{\mathrm{SN}} is defined as βSN≡Mg/(τSN​ψ)subscript𝛽SNsubscript𝑀gsubscript𝜏SN𝜓\beta_{\mathrm{SN}}\equiv M_{\mathrm{g}}/(\tau_{\mathrm{SN}}\psi), where Mgsubscript𝑀gM_{\mathrm{g}} is the total gas mass, τSNsubscript𝜏SN\tau_{\mathrm{SN}} is the timescale of dust destruction by supernova shocks, and ψ𝜓\psi is the SFR. This parameter can be expressed as follows (Hirashita, Tajiri, & Kamaya, 2002, equation 6):

βSN=ϵ​Ms​γψ​1XSF,subscript𝛽SNitalic-ϵsubscript𝑀s𝛾𝜓1subscript𝑋SF\displaystyle\beta_{\mathrm{SN}}=\epsilon M_{\mathrm{s}}\frac{\gamma}{\psi}\frac{1}{X_{\rm SF}}\,, (15)

where ϵitalic-ϵ\epsilon is the fraction of destroyed dust in a SN blast, Mssubscript𝑀sM_{\rm s} is the gas mass accelerated to a velocity large enough for dust destruction (typically 100 km s-1), γ𝛾\gamma is the supernova rate, and XSFsubscript𝑋SFX_{\rm SF} is the gas mass fraction in the star-forming region, where the dust formation and destruction are really occurring (the rest of the gas is considered to be contained in the H i envelope, which they assume not to be concerned with the dust formation and destruction). Typical values are ϵ∼0.1similar-toitalic-ϵ0.1\epsilon\sim 0.1 (McKee, 1989), Ms∼6800​M⊙similar-tosubscript𝑀s6800subscript𝑀direct-productM_{\rm s}\sim 6800M_{\odot} (if we adopt 1051superscript105110^{51} erg for the kinetic energy input of a supernova, and 100 km s-1 for the threshold velocity for the dust destruction), γ/ψ∼1/136​M⊙similar-to𝛾𝜓1136subscript𝑀direct-product\gamma/\psi\sim 1/136M_{\odot} (for the Galaxy; Lisenfeld & Ferrara (1998)), we obtain βSN=5subscript𝛽SN5\beta_{\mathrm{SN}}=5 for XSF=1subscript𝑋SF1X_{\rm SF}=1. Hirashita, Tajiri, & Kamaya (2002) argue that this parameter changes according to the relative contribution between Type Ia supernovae and Type II supernovae. If an intermittent star formation activity is assumed, γ/ψ𝛾𝜓\gamma/\psi can change by a factor of 20 (Bradamante, Matteucci, & D’Ercole, 1998; Hirashita, Tajiri, & Kamaya, 2002). Motivated by this factor, they changed βSNsubscript𝛽SN\beta_{\mathrm{SN}} from 1 to 25.

In Figure 2, we show the theoretical predictions for β=1𝛽1\beta=1, 5, and 25 with fin=0.1subscript𝑓in0.1f_{\rm in}=0.1. We observe that those models explains the data points except for the two extremes (II Zw 71 and Mrk 71 for the upper and lower extremes in Figure 2, respectively). The variation in βSNsubscript𝛽SN\beta_{\mathrm{SN}} increases the scatter of the dust-to-gas ratio at a certain metallicity and makes the correlation less clear. Further change of βSNsubscript𝛽SN\beta_{\rm SN} may be possible because of the change of XSFsubscript𝑋SFX_{\rm SF}. As mentioned in section 5.1, only a small fraction of gas may be concerned with star formation in Mrk 71. Thus, XSF≪1much-less-thansubscript𝑋SF1X_{\rm SF}\ll 1 is expected for Mrk 71, where βSNsubscript𝛽SN\beta_{\rm SN} could be larger than the above values. Such a large value of βSNsubscript𝛽SN\beta_{\rm SN} may explain the extremely poor dust-to-gas ratio of Mrk 71.

As commented above, the dust-to-gas ratios are larger if we adopt β=2𝛽2\beta=2, and/or if the cold dust component contributing to the submillimeter wavelengths, which we fail to trace in FIR, really exists as proposed by Galliano et al. (2005). In these cases, we should adopt a larger finsubscript𝑓inf_{\rm in}, but a large variation of βSNsubscript𝛽SN\beta_{\rm SN} is still required to explain the large scatter of dust-to-gas ratios.

6 Summary

We have reported far-infrared (FIR) properties of eight blue compact dwarf galaxies (BCDs) observed by AKARI. The fluxes at wavelengths of 65 μ𝜇\mum, 90 μ𝜇\mum, 140 μ𝜇\mum, and 160 μ𝜇\mum are measured and are used to estimate basic quantities about dust grains such as dust temperature, dust mass, and total FIR luminosity. We have found that the typical dust temperature of our BCD sample, except for Mrk 7 and II Zw 71, is significantly higher than that of normal spiral galaxies. This indicates high interstellar radiation field, which proves to range up to 100 times the Galactic value. This confirms the concentrated star-forming activity in BCDs. The star formation rate (SFR) is also evaluated from the FIR luminosity as 0.01–0.5 M⊙subscript𝑀direct-productM_{\odot} yr-1. Combining this quantity with gas mass taken from the literature, we estimate the gas consumption timescales (gas mass divided by SFR), which span a wide range from 1 Gyr to 100 Gyr. A natural interpretation of this large variety can be provided by intermittent star formation activity. We finally show the relation between dust-to-gas ratio and metallicity (we utilize our estimate of dust mass, and take other necessary quantities from the literature). There is a positive correlation between dust-to-gas ratio and metallicity as expected from chemical evolution models.
